text:
B: Hello. Can you hear me all right?
A: Yeah. Hiya.
B: Lee.
A: Bianca. I'm in Wolverhampton.
B: Hucknall, near Nottingham. What do you do, Bianca?
A: Erm, uni. Second year, Accounting and Finance.
B: Right. My daughter's at university. Sheffield. She's twenty.
A: Oh, same age as me. What's she doing?
B: Psychology.
A: I did that for A-level. It was alright. Kind of a lot of essays though.
B: That's what she says. She rings up when there's a deadline and she's panicking.
A: Yeah, mine are piling up at the minute. Three due in the same fortnight. I just do them in order, like, whichever's due first. No point stressing.
B: That's the right way to do it, I'd say. Do you live in halls, or at home?
A: Neither, I've got a flat with my boyfriend. In Bilston. Just above some shops.
B: Oh. Right. That's a big step at twenty.
A: It was cheaper, to be honest. Rent split two ways, bills split two ways. It works out.
B: Have you sat down and done the figures?
A: Yeah, I've got a spreadsheet. Everything goes on it. Rent, food, his bits, my bits. I'm kind of strict with it.
B: Good. I do ours in Excel. The whole household budget, and I've got one for the pension as well, for when I retire.
A: When's that?
B: Sixty-two, if the sums add up. So twelve years.
A: That's quite organised.
B: It saves surprises. My wife says I'm a bit much with it.
A: No, I get it. My mum was always skint when I was younger, so I check everything. I'd rather know.
B: Yes. That's sensible. What are you going to do after?
A: Placement in Birmingham, hopefully. Then ACCA. Then just, earn properly, do you know what I mean.
B: Nothing wrong with that. Steady work. I've been in the same place nineteen years.
A: Nineteen? Doing what?
B: Quality. I inspect aerospace parts on a measuring machine. If they're out by a few microns, I write it up.
A: Microns. Is that, like, tiny?
B: Thousandths of a millimetre.
A: That'd do my head in.
B: You get used to it. It's like your spreadsheet. It either adds up or it doesn't.
A: Yeah, that's true actually.
B: Do you get back to see your family much? Living in the flat.
A: My mum's only fifteen minutes away. She sends me home with loads of food every time. Like, tubs and tubs.
B: My wife does that with Megan. Puts a cob in her bag for the train.
A: A cob?
B: Bread roll.
A: Oh, we say bap. My mum sends soup, mostly. Romanian stuff.
B: Well, she won't go hungry, then.
A: No. I've got a freezer full.
